segments.text: There's an AI model called Jev that can't chat or write code. All it does is pick an answer from
a list. And a lot of people got very excited about it. We hand it some text and a few options,
and it tells us which option fits and how sure it is. Spam or not spam. Happy customer or angry
one. Billing problem or technical problem. Some of us shrugged because we've had classifiers for
decades, others had it playing Tetris. Same model, yes, Tetris.
So is it boring, or is it a big deal? To figure that out, let's look at how machines
learn to sort text in the first place. It's hard to judge Gev without knowing what came
before it.
Classification just means sorting. A pile of text goes in, a label comes out. Email goes
to spam or inbox. A review goes to positive or negative. A support ticket goes to billing
or tech. Computers are good with numbers, and sentences are messy. They can be 10 words
long or 10,000. The classic sorting tools need an input of one fixed size, so the first
job is always the same. We have to turn messy text into a neat row of numbers.
numbers. The oldest answer is also the simplest. We list every word in our training data, say
50,000 words. Every word gets its own slot. Then, for any message, we count. How many
times does free appear? How about refund? We end up with a row of 50,000 numbers, mostly
zeros. A short message and a long one give us the same size row. This is called a bag
of words. Think of it as tossing the whole message in a bag and counting what's inside.
Then a simple model, naive Bayes or logistic regression, learns which words lean toward
which label. Winner and prize push towards spam. Attached and meeting push the other way.
And it works pretty well. Text sorting like this goes back to the early 60s
and it's been behind plenty of spam filters. On movie reviews it gets about 90% right.
It's fast, it's cheap, and we can bill one in an afternoon.
But there's a problem. We lost the word order. The dog bites the man, and the man bites the
dog make the exact same row of numbers, even though one is ordinary and the other is news.
The fix came in two parts. First, we stop giving words a slot in a list and give each
word a short string of numbers instead. This is called an embedding. Words used in similar
ways get similar numbers, so good ends up near great and far from awful.
One flaw, a word gets the same numbers everywhere. Bank looks identical in riverbank and bank
account.
Second, we build a network that reads the words in order. The classic one is the recurrent
network. It reads one word at a time and keeps a running summary, like someone holding the
gist of a sentence in their head. Each new word updates the gist, so order matters now.
shuffle the words and the gist comes out different.
There's a catch, that summary has a fixed size,
so in the long text the early parts get squeezed out.
These networks were also slow since each step waits for the last one
and they were famously painful to train.
Then in 2018, a method called ULMfit showed a better way.
Don't start from zero.
First train the network on a huge pile of ordinary text
so it learns how language works,
then fine-tune it on the small task we care about.
Movie review accuracy jumped to around 95%.
Remember that idea. Train big first, then fine-tune small.
It keeps coming back. There was another option too.
Convolutional networks, the kind used for images,
can slide a small window across a sentence, three words at a time,
hunting for patterns like surprisingly good acting.
They're quick because every window can be checked at once.
On reviews, they did about as well as the old bag of words. Decent, but nothing special.
Then in 2017, the Transformer arrived. Its big trick is attention. Every word can look
straight at every other word and decide which ones matter. There's no fading summary to
worry about. Bank can look at river and know which kind of bank it is. Two families grew
out of it. Encoder models, like BERT, read text in both directions and are built to understand.
They put a special marker at the front, and once the model has read everything,
that marker holds a summary we can hook a small classifier onto.
Decoder models, like GPT, read left to right and predict the next word. They're built to right.
For a while, encoders were their natural sorters, and decoders were the writers.
Then it turned out decoders could sort well too.
We can just ask, is this review positive or negative?
A big enough model answers.
No training needed.
The problem is that it's sloppy.
We want one clean label and sometimes we get a whole paragraph.
And we're paying for a giant model to do a small job.
So a lot of teams went with a less exciting option.
They took a modern encoder like modern BERT, added a small classification head and fine
tuned it. With almost no effort, that gets around 95% on movie reviews. Even a small
GPT-2 sized model reaches about 92%. So by now we had two options, and a rule of thumb
for picking. Option one was to ask a big general model every time. No training, super flexible.
But it's slow, and it costs real money at scale. Option two was to fine tune a small
model for the job. Fast and cheap to run. But we need labelled data, a training run
and a brand new model for every new problem. The rule was simple. For a one-off question,
ask the big model. For the same task a million times, train our own.
But that left a gap. What we wanted was something quick and cheap that works on any question
without training. That's the gap Jeff steps into.
Quick break. If this is helping, please subscribe to the channel.
Re-explain AI topics in plain English, with no jargon, so none of it sounds like a foreign
language.
OK, back to Jeff. Jeff comes from a company called TypeSafe AI. We send it text, plus
a question with some possible answers. It sends back its pick and probabilities. They
claim it matches the big lunar class models on decision tasks, while being far faster
and far cheaper. There are three question types. The first is choice, which picks one answer
from a list. The second is no-yul, a yes or no question, where we get a probability for
yes. Ask several no-yul questions at once and we can handle texts that fit more than
one label. The third is score, which grades something against a rubric like 0, 1 or 2.
For movie reviews, we paste in the review, ask what's the overall sentiment, and
describe each option in plain words. Negative means an unfavourable opinion, positive means
a favourable one. That comes positive, a confidence number and a probability for each option.
When people ran all 25,000 test reviews through it, it got about 96.5% right. It took around
20 minutes and cost about 65 cents. That's slightly ahead of a fine-tuned modern BERT
with no training run. A couple of caveats. We can't tell whether those reviews were
in its training data, and the runs aren't perfectly repeatable. Same input, slightly
different totals. That's normal for models served at scale.
This next part surprised a lot of people. If we swap the question, the same model can
play Tetris in real time. Every move is just a choice from a short list. Left, right,
rotate, drop. The fine-tuned sentiment model can't do that without starting over.
Nobody outside the company knows how Jeff is built, so this part is a guess. But
there's a simple trick that could make a model like this work. Normally, a
classifier has one output per label. Two labels, two outputs. Want a third label?
Rebuild the model. The trick is to use only one output. For each option, we show
the model three things – the text, the instructions, and that option's description. It reads them
and produces a single number for how well the option fits. We do this for every option,
squash the scores into probabilities with Softmax, and take the top one.
Three options means three passes through the same scorer. Seven options, seven passes. The model
doesn't mind either way. The labels are just part of the input now, so they can change every time.
That part is easy to build. The hard part is making it work on tasks it has never seen.
And that comes down to training data.
The company says its data is entirely synthetic, but carefully made, not just dumped out of
a chatbot. If that's true, most of the effort went into the data. That fits something people
in machine learning have seen for years. When a model isn't good enough, better data usually
helps more than another week of tweaking settings.
The part we find most interesting isn't flashy at all. It's the probabilities.
Say a model calls a review 74% positive. That number should mean something. If we collect
a hundred reviews that got a 74, about 74 should truly be positive. That's calibration.
Neural networks are usually bad at it. They sound sure about everything. A 74 and a 54
or both give the label positive, but we treat them very differently.
We could trust the first one. The second should go to a person.
One fix is temperature scaling. We divide the model's raw scores by a single number before
the softmax, tuned on held-out data. It changes how sure the model sounds, not which answer
it picks.
TypeSafe says it trains for honesty directly, with a method it calls RLCD. The details
our secret, but a published idea points the same way, called RLCR. Normally, in this kind
of reinforcement learning, a right answer earns one point, and a wrong one earns zero. RLCR
also asks the model to state how likely it is to be right, then subtracts the squared gap between
that confidence and what actually happened. Here's how that plays out. 90% sure and right,
That scores 0.99. 90% sure and wrong, minus 0.81, almost a whole point lost for Swagger.
20% sure and wrong, minus 0.04, a tiny slap because it knew it might be wrong.
So the model's best move is to be honest about what it knows. In that paper, calibration error
on one test dropped from 0.37 to 0.03, with about the same accuracy. We don't know if
The question is whether normal training already does this. In theory, yes. In practice, networks
overfit their confidence. They can get more and more certain on training data without
getting any more correct on new data. So, extra tricks sometimes help a little, and we always
have to check.
Soon after Gev launched, hundreds of clones appeared. Most take a small model, fine-tune
it on sorting examples, and wrap a Gev-looking API around it. That's the easy part.
When people tested a couple of the better ones on the movie reviews, one scored about 83% and another about 92%.
Neither could handle the Tetris test. Handling lots of different tasks is the hard part, and that's what set Jev apart from the copies.
An open version would still be a big deal, mostly for privacy. Plenty of text can't be sent to someone else's servers.
The big labs noticed too. OpenAI announced its own version, the Decisions API, built on Luna.
It has weak spots too. Reportedly, Gev struggles with legal review in languages other than
English, though a cheap translation step in front can patch that.
And for one narrow task at huge volume, a custom fine-tuned model still wins on speed
and accuracy.
Where would we use it? The obvious ones are sorting email and routing support tickets.
They could also check text for prompt injection before it reaches an AI agent, or decide how
hard a big model should think, or pick which instruction file an agent should load, or act
as a judge when we test other models. None of that is a new ability, though. Classifiers are old.
What changed is how hard it is to get one. It used to take a labelled dataset and a training run.
Now it takes a sentence describing what we want. So the bar for building our own model is much
higher than it was. And if small, fast models handle the little choices inside bigger AI
systems, the expensive models only get called when they're really needed. That could make
AI agents cheaper and quicker. So is it just a boring tool? Kind of. It's the same old
sorting job. We just get to ask for it in plain English now, and the answer comes back
almost instantly.
